title: Chapter 30: The Morning Dew 3
content:
Chapter 30

Chang Ping, the clan leader of the Yueyang Chang Clan, had been away with a few family members on an extended night-hunt lasting over half a month when the devastating news reached him. Dropping everything, he rushed back, only to be met with nightmare and ash. Once the initial shock faded, the only clue he uncovered was that someone had maliciously smashed their protective barrier and loosed a ravenous swarm of dark wraiths into the compound. Beyond that, it was a complete dead end.

Normally, the downfall of a minor backwater clan wouldn't make waves across the cultivation world. But the timing was uniquely volatile: the Sunshot Campaign had ended long ago, and the grand siege of the Burial Mounds had only just wrapped up. The political climate was walking on eggshells, pretending everything was peaceful, so this sudden bloodbath set the entire cultivation community on fire. A handful of loud sensationalists immediately began spinning rumors that the Yiling Patriarch, Wei Wuxian, had crawled out of his grave for payback. Yet with zero evidence and no leads, the killer slipped clean away.

Xiao Xingchen, naturally, was not the type of man to look the other way. He took up the case on his own initiative, determined to drag the truth into the light for Chang Ping. A month later, he cornered the butcher.

His name was Xue Yang.

Xue Yang was actually younger than Xiao Xingchen—a boy, plain and simple. Yet that fresh youth didn't soften his vicious edge in the slightest. From fifteen on, he’d ruled the roost as Kuizhou’s most notorious thug. He had a disarming, dimpled smile, but behind those grinning cheeks lay a sadistic, venomous streak so black that merely whispering his name was enough to make locals blanch. Having lived rough on the streets in his childhood, he’d run into some ugly friction with Chang Ping’s father—and had nursed that grudge for years. Pure spite, spiced with a few unspoken motives, had culminated in this horrific bloodbath.

Once Xiao Xingchen unraveled the truth, he hunted the boy down across three full provinces, finally pinning Xue Yang while he was casually loafing about, picking street brawls without a care in the world. Taking advantage of a massive Discussion Conference hosted by the Lanling Jin Clan atop Carp Tower—where all the great families had gathered to debate the Dao—Xiao Xingchen hauled the punk straight before the crowd, laid out the gruesome details, and demanded justice.

His evidence was airtight. Virtually every sect leader nodded in agreement, ready to drop the hammer.

Only one clan pushed back with everything they had: the Lanling Jin Clan.

"Pushing back in a room like that is practically painting a target on your own back," Wei Wuxian mused, brow furrowing. "Was this Xue Yang some golden boy in Jin Guangshan's inner circle?"

"A guest disciple," Lan Wangji replied.

"A guest disciple?" Wei Wuxian echoed, genuinely baffled. "The Lanling Jin Clan was already sitting pretty in the top four back then. Why on earth would they hire a street hoodlum as an honored guest?"

Lan Wangji’s voice was measured. "That is the second connection."

His pale eyes locked dead onto Wei Wuxian’s, dropping the final piece into place: "The Yin Tiger Tally."

Wei Wuxian’s stomach plummeted into freefall.

Those three words weren't just familiar—nobody on this earth knew that ungodly talisman better than the man who forged it.

Out of every terrifying dark relic he had conjured in his previous life, the Yin Tiger Tally was hands-down the most lethal—and the one prize every single clan salivated over.

A tiger tally was traditionally an imperial seal used to command troops. True to its name, whoever held the Yin Tiger Tally could herd legions of corpses, phantoms, and spiteful dead like an unstoppable army.

Truth be told, Wei Wuxian hadn't thought that far ahead when he forged it. Micromanaging hordes of walking corpses using only his own spiritual consciousness was exhausting, and mental burnout hit hard. Remembering a chunk of rare, purified iron ore he’d once carved out of a demonic beast’s gut, he’d melted it down and hammered it into a classic tiger seal.

He tested it once.

And in that single breath, he realized he’d summoned a monster.

The sheer, terrifying firepower of the tally blew past his wildest calculations. He’d built it as a utility tool, but the artifact’s raw malice began creeping upward, threatening to swallow its creator whole. Worse, it didn't recognize a master. It carried zero loyalty. Good, evil, friend, foe—it didn't care whose palm held it; whoever gripped the metal held the leash.

The catastrophe was already wrought, and Wei Wuxian had genuinely tried to melt it down. But forging a relic like that was hard; destroying it was ten times harder, demanding monstrous amounts of spiritual energy and time he simply didn't have. Besides, he’d already sensed the wolves circling at his back, knowing the day would come when the entire world would hunt him down. The tally’s sheer deterrent power was the only reason the great clans didn't kick his doors in overnight.

So, he shelved the destruction, splitting the tally into two halves so its magic could only ignite when the pieces clicked together. And he swore never to draw it unless backed into an absolute corner.

He only ever deployed it twice. And both times, the earth drank rivers of blood.

The first was during the Sunshot Campaign. The second shook him so deeply that he gritted his teeth and permanently shattered one of the halves to dust. But before he could melt the second piece, the siege of the Burial Mounds came crashing down. What happened to the scrap after that wasn't his problem anymore.

Having poured his own soul into that iron, Wei Wuxian would bet his life on one cold fact: even if the clan that looted it set the half-tally on a golden altar, burning high-grade incense and bowing to it day and night, a single piece was nothing more than an expensive paperweight.

Yet Lan Wangji had just dropped a bombshell: this brat, Xue Yang, seemed to have figured out how to reconstruct the missing half!

Young as he was, Xue Yang possessed a terrifying, wicked brilliance—a crooked prodigy of the highest order. The Lanling Jin Clan discovered that by using the surviving piece as a blueprint, he could cobble together a functional replica of the other half. The knockoff was fragile and lacked the crushing firepower of the original, but it still packed enough horror to turn the world upside down.

The puzzle pieces clicked. "So the Jin Clan needed Xue Yang alive to finish their little toy," Wei Wuxian said, a sour taste in his mouth. "Of course they shielded him."

Wiping out the Chang Clan might not have just been petty payback for getting slapped around as a street rat. For all they knew, Xue Yang had used those dozens of living, breathing mortals as guinea pigs to test the lethality of his bootleg Yin Tiger Tally!

No wonder rumors had tied the massacre right back to his name. Wei Wuxian could practically hear the pious sects grinding their teeth through their high-and-mighty scolding:“That bastard Wei Wuxian! If he hadn't built that cursed thing in the first place, none of this blood would be on our hands!”

Pulling his thoughts back, they returned to Carp Tower.

The Lanling Jin Clan was dead-set on covering for their weapon-smith, but Xiao Xingchen wasn't a man who could be swayed by honeyed words or blunt threats. The standoff dragged on until it caught the attention of Chifeng-zun, Nie Mingjue, who hadn't even attended the conference. Riding his sabre, he dropped straight out of the sky into Koi Tower to handle it in person.

Nie Mingjue was technically a junior to Jin Guangshan, but his spine was forged from iron. He had zero tolerance for corruption, and the blistering tongue-lashing he unleashed left Jin Guangshan pale, humiliated, and speechless. Hot-tempered as ever, Nie Mingjue drew his sabre right there in the hall, ready to lop Xue Yang’s head off on the spot. His sworn brother Jin Guangyao—Lianfang-zun—hurried forward to smooth things over, only for Nie Mingjue to bark at him to get lost, scolding him so viciously that Jin Guangyao shrank behind Lan Xichen, not daring to peep another syllable. In the end, cornered and outmaneuvered, the Jin Clan had no choice but to fold.

From the moment he was dragged into the hall, Xue Yang had worn an insufferable, smug smirk. Even with a heavy sabre hovering inches from his windpipe, his grin never faltered. As the guards hauled him down toward the dungeons, he’d actually turned back, offering Xiao Xingchen an oily, sickeningly sweet farewell:“Daozhang, don't you go forgetting me now. We'll see who gets the last laugh.”

Hearing that, Wei Wuxian’s stomach tightened. A petty lunatic's'we'll see'was going to cost Xiao Xingchen everything.

The Lanling Jin Clan truly had the thickest skin in the four corners of the earth. They’d nodded along in front of hundreds of witnesses, promising an execution, but the second Nie Mingjue turned his back, they tossed Xue Yang into a private cell, quietly commuting the death sentence to life imprisonment. Catching wind of the bait-and-switch, Nie Mingjue flew into a rage, ramping up political pressure, but the Jin Clan dragged their feet, dodging and stonewalling at every turn. The other families simply folded their arms to watch the fireworks.

And then, out of nowhere, Nie Mingjue suffered catastrophic qi deviation and died.

He’d advanced his cultivation faster than any previous Nie Clan leader, and he’d died younger than any of them, too.

With their fiercest critic six feet under, the Lanling Jin Clan dropped all pretense, letting their greed off the leash. Jin Guangshan began plotting ways to bust Xue Yang out of the dungeon so they could get back to reverse-engineering the Yin Tiger Tally.

Still, high society demanded decorum. Pulling a mass murderer out of prison required a squeaky-clean pretext, or the blowback would be messy.

So, their eyes shifted onto Chang Ping.

Between relentless intimidation and mountains of silver, the Jin Clan’s campaign wore the man down. Chang Ping broke, recanting every single charge he’d ever filed and publicly declaring:The massacre of the Chang Clan had nothing to do with Xue Yang.

Xiao Xingchen rushed to his door the moment the news broke, demanding answers.

Chang Ping could only offer a hollow, defeated grimace:“What else am I supposed to do? If I don't swallow this, the few surviving members of my family won't live to see next month. I'm grateful for your help, Daozhang, but... please, just leave it alone. Helping me now is practically signing my death warrant. I don't want the Yueyang Chang Clan wiped from the earth for good.”

Just like that, the beast was unleashed back into the wild.

Wei Wuxian walked on in heavy silence.

Had he been in Chang Ping’s shoes, it wouldn't matter if the Lanling Jin Clan ruled the heavens or promised him endless mountains of gold and glory—he would never have recanted a single syllable. Instead, he would’ve slipped into that dungeon in the dead of night, sliced Xue Yang into a pile of raw mince, summoned the bastard's soul right back into the meat, and minced him again and again until the punk cursed the day his mother birthed him.

Yet not everyone was wired with his self-destructive, scorched-earth obstinacy. Chang Ping still had surviving kin to protect. He was young, unmarried, childless, and had barely taken his first steps along the immortal path. Whether threatened with the slaughter of his remaining family or the total ruin of his personal future, he’d had to make the practical calculation.

At the end of the day, Wei Wuxian wasn't Chang Ping. He couldn't carry the man's righteous fury, and he certainly couldn't carry the crushing terror and torment that broke him.

Once free of his chains, Xue Yang naturally returned for his pound of flesh. Only this time, he didn't target Xiao Xingchen directly.

Xiao Xingchen had descended his mountain alone, carrying no family name and no clan behind him. His only anchor in the mortal realm was a companion he’d met after descending: a man named Song Lan. Song Lan was another celebrated Daoist cultivator of the era—proud, noble, and untainted by scandal. Both men dreamed of founding a sect built on shared ideals rather than blood ties; they were true kindred spirits, cutting through the world side by side. Back then, people toasted them with an admiring couplet:Xiao Xingchen, the bright moon and gentle breeze; Song Zichen, the proud snow and biting frost.

So Xue Yang aimed his venom there. Pulling the exact same trick, he slaughtered Baixue Temple—the mountain monastery where Song Lan had grown up and trained—leaving not a single survivor. And to top it off, he ambushed Song Lan from the shadows, hurling corrosive poison powder that burned the man's eyes straight out of his skull.

Having already butchered one sect, Xue Yang executed the massacre with chilling efficiency, scrubbing the scene so clean not a shred of physical evidence remained. Everyone with a brain knew who held the blade, but what could they do? There was no proof. With Jin Guangshan running political interference and Nie Mingjue dead in the ground, not a single person had the spine to touch him.

Hearing the tale wind down, an odd thought nudged at Wei Wuxian's mind: Lan Wangji might look like an aloof ice sculpture, but knowing the man’s character, his hatred of corruption burned just as hot as Nie Mingjue’s ever did. Back in the day, whenever the Jin Clan threw their weight around, Lan Wangji never hesitated to call them out to their faces. Even now, he rarely bothered showing up to their grand conferences, completely refusing to indulge their vanity. If two horrific massacres had rocked the realm back-to-back, sparking public outrage, Lan Wangji would never have sat on his hands. Why hadn't he stepped in to put Xue Yang in his place?

He opened his mouth to ask, only for the memory of those savage discipline scars across Lan Wangji’s back to flash behind his eyes.

A single lash from a discipline whip was enough to leave a man bedridden for weeks. If Lan Wangji had taken over thirty strikes, the punishment must have been followed by years of forced isolation and agonizing recovery. The years of Xue Yang's rampage were likely the exact years Lan Wangji was locked away, nursing shattered flesh.

No wonder he’d only "heard whispers" of the incident.

A quiet ache pulled at Wei Wuxian’s chest over those hidden scars. Knowing it wasn't his place to pry, he swallowed the question, gently steering the topic back: "And what happened to Daozhang Xiao Xingchen after that?"

What happened? A tragedy, naturally.

When Xiao Xingchen originally bade farewell to his master, he had sworn an unbreakable oath never to return. He held oaths sacred, yet seeing Song Lan blinded and teetering on the edge of death, he broke his vow without a second thought. Hoisting Song Lan onto his back, he climbed back up the misty peaks to Baoshan Sanren's sanctuary, begging his master to save his friend.

Moved by their bond, Baoshan Sanren granted the plea. Xiao Xingchen descended the mountain alone and vanished into the mist, never to be seen again.

A year later, Song Lan emerged from the mountains. The cultivation world was shocked to discover that his destroyed eyes had been miraculously healed, seeing the sun once more. But in truth, it had nothing to do with divine medicine: Xiao Xingchen had gouged out his own eyes, gifting them to the friend he had dragged into his nightmare.

Song Lan burned for vengeance, but by then, Jin Guangshan had kicked the bucket, and Jin Guangyao had taken the reins of the Lanling Jin Clan, ascending to the seat of Chief Cultivator. To project a squeaky-clean image for his new regime, his very first move was to execute a sweeping purge of Xue Yang. He buried all mention of restoring the Yin Tiger Tally, rolled out lavish reparations to smooth ruffled feathers, and clamped down on tavern gossip. Song Lan set off to scour the realm for his lost friend; for a while, rumors would pop up that he’d passed through this town or that ridge, but eventually, even those whispers dried up. Couple that with the fact that the Yueyang Chang Clan was a tiny, forgotten family, and the entire tragedy was slowly swept under the rug of time.

Hearing the long, bitter chronicle come to a close, Wei Wuxian let out a low, heavy exhale, feeling an ache of hollow regret. "To lose everything over a disaster you were only trying to fix... What a cruel hand. If only Xiao Xingchen had been born a few years earlier, or if I had hung on a few years longer, maybe things wouldn't have played out like this. If I’d been around, there’s no way in hell I would've stood by and let that happen. A man like that—I would've loved to share a drink with him!"

He caught himself, barking a dry, self-deprecating laugh.Me? Step in? How would I have managed that? If I’d been alive, they wouldn't have even bothered investigating the Chang Clan—they would've pinned the whole massacre on my head before the bodies were even cold. And if I’d bumped into Daozhang Xiao Xingchen on the road and tried to buy him a drink, he probably would've smacked me upside the head with his whisk!

They had already left the Chang estate behind, reaching a lonely graveyard tucked along the outskirts. Spotting the faded crimson character forChangcarved into an archway, Wei Wuxian asked, "So how did Chang Ping die in the end? Who butchered the survivors withlingchi?"

Before Lan Wangji could reply, a muffledthud-thud-thudrolled through the twilight.

It sounded strikingly like frantic pounding on a wooden door, yet muffled, rhythmic, and relentless—as though smothered beneath a heavy layer of dirt.

Both men went instantly still.

Over fifty souls of the Yueyang Chang Clan lay buried beneath these mounds, battering their fists against their coffin lids from the inside. Just like that horrific night when they were scared to death, they were slamming against the wood, praying for an unlatching that would never come.

It was the very phenomenon the wine server had described: the coffin-battering of the Chang cemetery!

Yet the boy had sworn the hauntings had stopped a decade ago. Why on earth were the graves throwing a fit the exact second they arrived?

Masking their spiritual presence as one, Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji crept into the shadows without a breath of sound.

Peeking from behind the stone pillar of the archway, they saw it: dead center in the cemetery, surrounded by weathered headstones, gaped a fresh pit.

It was dug remarkably deep, dark mounds of freshly turned earth piled high along the lip. Faint scraping rustled from the depths.

Someone was grave-robbing.

Holding their breath, the two waited in absolute silence for the digger to show his face.

Less than half an incense stick later, two figures vaulted lightly out of the pit.

It took sharp eyes to realize it was actually two bodies; they were practically fused together, one hauling the other across his back in a tight piggyback, both swathed in matching pitch-black robes.

The one standing on his own two feet had his back turned, broad-shouldered and long-limbed. The passenger on his shoulders hung completely limp, head and limbs dangling without a breath of vitality—which made sense; hauled straight out of a tomb, a corpse had no business looking alive.

Right as the thought crossed Wei Wuxian’s mind, the grave-robber whipped his head around, locking eyes with them.

Swirling over the intruder's face was an oily, roiling cloud of pitch-black smoke, masking his features in total obscurity!

Wei Wuxian knew instantly that this man had cloaked his face in some bizarre obscuring spell. Bichen cleared its scabbard, and Lan Wangji swept across the graveyard like a flash of winter frost, trading strikes with the intruder in a heartbeat. The gravedigger’s reflexes were frighteningly sharp; seeing the cerulean sword-glare lunging for his throat, he pinched a hand seal, conjuring his own streak of spiritual light to parry. Yet his blade, much like his face, was wrapped in thick, churning black smog, rendering its true hue and spiritual edge entirely unreadable. Weighed down by a corpse slung across his shoulders, the intruder fought with an awkward, off-balance posture. After their sword-glares clashed half a dozen times, Lan Wangji drew Bichen back, his fingers tightening around the hilt as a layer of arctic frost settled across his features.

Wei Wuxian caught on immediately. Even to an outside observer, the tell was blindingly obvious: this masked gravedigger was intimately familiar with Lan Wangji’s sword forms!

Without a word, Lan Wangji thrust forward with crushing force, his spiritual pressure rolling across the graveyard like a mountain range collapsing inward. The intruder retreated step by step, clearly aware that saddled with dead weight, he was no match for Lan Wangji and faced imminent capture. His hand dipped toward his sash, fishing out a deep blue talisman.

A Transportation Talisman!

A charm like that could catapult a cultivator thousands of miles in the blink of an eye, but the spiritual tax was monstrous; it drained a practitioner’s core so severely that recovery took an eternity, and anyone lacking top-tier reserves couldn't even ignite it. While precious beyond measure, practically no one used them. Spotting his intent to bolt, Wei Wuxian clapped his hands twice in rapid succession, dropped to one knee, and drove a solid fist straight into the earth!

The concussive shockwave ripped through layers of soil, punching deep into the subterranean chambers and shattering the heavy coffin lids below, shocking the restless dead within to madness. With a wet, violent crunch, four bloody arms burst through the dirt, clamping around the gravedigger’s ankles like iron vices!

The intruder didn't flinch, channeling a burst of spiritual energy down to his heels that instantly pulverized the skeletal grip. Unsheathing his bamboo flute, Wei Wuxian blew a piercing, shrieking note that tore through the falling dusk; two rotting corpses breached the soil completely, slithering up the gravedigger's shins like serpents to sink their yellowed teeth straight into his neck and arms!

The intruder let out a contemptuous scoff, as if mocking child's play, and flooded his meridians with concussive force. Yet the moment the spiritual burst shattered the corpses, his eyes went wide behind the smoke—he'd been played.

The concussive wave had blasted the corpse right off his back!

Wei Wuxian slapped a tombstone, cackling with unhinged glee. Lan Wangji caught the limp, sprawling body with one arm, his other thrusting Bichen forward in a lethal arc. Seeing his hard-won prize snatched away, and thoroughly outmatched in a straight duel—especially with someone running interference from the dark—the gravedigger didn't dare linger. He slammed the Transportation Talisman against the grass. A deafening crack shook the air as a pillar of blue flame roared toward the clouds, swallowing his silhouette whole.

Wei Wuxian had known the man was holding a Transportation Talisman; even if they pinned him down, he would have found an angle to vanish. Leaving behind the corpse he’d risked life and limb to exhume was already a massive win, so there was no point crying over spilled milk.

Ambling over, he peered down at Lan Wangji's arms. "Let's see what he dug up."

A closer look made his eyebrows shoot up. The corpse's head had cracked wide open, but spilling from the fracture wasn't gore or rotted brain matter—it was clump after clump of yellowed, blackened cotton batting!

With a light tug, the head popped clean off. Dangling the exquisitely crafted mannequin skull by its hair, Wei Wuxian blinked. "What's the gag here? The Chang cemetery is housing a glorified scarecrow stuffed with rags and cotton?"

Having caught the dead weight earlier, Lan Wangji had already noted the discrepancy. "Not entirely fake."

Wei Wuxian gave the body a thorough pat-down. The limbs were soft and pliable, but the chest and abdomen felt like solid, unyielding iron. Ripping open the burial shroud, the truth was laid bare: the torso was flesh and bone; everything else was dummy padding.

The fabric limbs and stuffed head were placed there simply to trick the torso's spiritual instincts, making the severed core believe it was still attached to a complete body. Judging by the muscular build and the jagged cross-section at the left shoulder, this was undeniably the torso of their dear friend. That gravedigger had risked everything tonight just to unearth it.

Straightening up, Wei Wuxian rubbed his chin. "Looks like whoever hid the pieces realized we're on the hunt and rushed here to relocate the torso before we sniffed it out. Fortune favors the bold—they picked the exact second we strolled in! But tell me..." His voice dropped into a lower register. "How in the world did that smoky-faced gravedigger know your clan's sword forms down to the millimeter?"

The frost on Lan Wangji’s face hadn't thawed; clearly, the exact same realization was gnawing at his thoughts.

Wei Wuxian continued, "The man's spiritual reserves are staggering—enough to burn a Transportation Talisman without passing out on the spot. And he went through the trouble of masking his face and his blade. Masking the face is standard tradecraft to avoid getting recognized. But an ordinary nobody has no reason to hide their sword-glare—unless that sword carries a massive reputation across the sects, so distinct that drawing steel would immediately blow his cover wide open."

Wei Wuxian leaned in slightly, his tone carefully probing. "Hanguang-jun, you traded strikes with him just now. Did he feel like someone... familiar?"

He swallowed the names resting on the tip of his tongue. Names like Lan Xichen. Or Lan Qiren.

Lan Wangji’s answer was absolute: "No."

Wei Wuxian trusted Lan Wangji’s word implicitly. The Second Young Master Lan was not the sort of man to bury his head in the sand or flinch from ugly realities. If he said no, then it was a definitive no. The man was allergic to lying anyway; Wei Wuxian figured that if forced to tell a falsehood, Lan Wangji would rather slap a Silence Spell on his own mouth and choke on the quiet.

With those two prominent figures struck from the board, Wei Wuxian let out a low whistle. "Well, that just made things ten times messier."

Lan Wangji slipped the torso into another reinforced Evil-Quelling Qiankun pouch, securing the seals with practiced efficiency. After sweeping the perimeter for any leftover traces, the pair took a slow, quiet trek back toward the tavern district.

The young server had kept his word. While eight out of ten wine houses down the lane had already shuttered their gates for the night, their shop's red banner was still proudly catching the night breeze, the lanterns glowing warmly. The boy was sitting out on the steps, shoveling rice from a massive bowl, his face splitting into a grin the second they rounded the corner. "You made it back! See? Told you we'd keep the doors open! Catch a glimpse of anything spooky out there?"

Wei Wuxian laughed it off with a few noncommittal jokes, guiding Lan Wangji back to their previous table.

With clay jugs lining the floorboards and crowding the table, Wei Wuxian cracked the seal on a fresh jar. "Right, where were we before that gravedigger popped out of nowhere to ruin our chat? I still haven't heard how Chang Ping actually met his maker."

Lan Wangji resumed the chronicle, his prose stripped of all decoration, cool and direct.

Years after the storm had cleared—with Xue Yang, Xiao Xingchen, and Song Lan either missing, scattered, or dead—the hammer finally fell. One morning, Chang Ping and the surviving members of his household were discovered slaughtered, their flesh carved away bylingchi. And, just like Song Lan before him, Chang Ping's eyes had been gouged from his skull.

This time around, no one could crack the mystery; every key player from the original tragedy had vanished off the face of the earth.

Yet one detail was verified beyond a shadow of a doubt.

The blade that executed that gruesome butchery, verified by the precise incisions along the bone, belonged to none other than Xiao Xingchen—the sacred sword, Shuanghua.

Wei Wuxian’s wine bowl paused inches from his lips, his expression genuinely shaken. "Carved up by Xiao Xingchen's own sword?! Was he really the one swinging it?"

"Xiao Xingchen is missing," Lan Wangji answered quietly. "No conclusion has been drawn."

"If the living man is nowhere to be found, did anyone attempt Inquiry?"

"It was attempted. No response."

No response meant only two things: either he was still breathing somewhere out there, or his soul had been pulverized so thoroughly it had ceased to exist.

When it came to the necromantic arts, Wei Wuxian couldn't help weighing in. "Spirit-summoning is an imprecise craft. You need the right stars, the right soil, and the right conduit—slip up on any of those and the line goes cold. I take it most people chalked it up to Xiao Xingchen's bloody revenge? What about you, Hanguang-jun? What's your take?"

Lan Wangji shook his head gently. "Without knowing the whole picture, I will not pass judgment."

Wei Wuxian smiled softly into his wine, thoroughly admiring that quiet, unbending integrity.

"And your thoughts?" Lan Wangji asked, eyes meeting his.

Wei Wuxian considered it. "Death by a thousand cuts is a punitive execution; the method itself screams retribution. And scooping out a man's eyes makes it almost impossible not to think of Xiao Xingchen, who gave up his own sight. It makes sense that folks would assume it was payback. But..." He paused, picking his words with care. "I don't think Xiao Xingchen stepped into that mess in the first place hoping for Chang Ping's gratitude. If it were me..."

Before he could finish the thought, the server scurried over, eagerly dropping two fresh plates of salted peanuts onto the table.

The interruption was almost a relief, saving him from digging any deeper. Looking across at Lan Wangji, Wei Wuxian chuckled. "What are you staring at me like that for, Hanguang-jun? I'm fine. I don't know the whole picture either, so I won't pass judgment. You hit the nail on the head: until every card is on the table, nobody has the right to point fingers. That said, I only asked for five jars, but you bought ten. I can't put away this much on my own. How about a cup? We're far beyond the Cloud Recesses; nobody's going to cane you for breaking curfew."

He was fully braced for an icy rejection, but Lan Wangji simply murmured, "Pour."

Wei Wuxian nearly choked. "Look at you, Hanguang-jun. You really have changed. Back in our school days, if I dared crack open a jar in front of you, you looked ready to throttle me, threatened to pitch me over the perimeter wall, and drew steel. And now here you are, stashing Emperor's Smile under your floorboards and sneaking sips in the dark!"

Lan Wangji smoothed his lapel, his voice untouched by ripples. "The Emperor's Smile remains untouched."

"If you're not drinking it, why dig a hole to hide it? Saving it as a welcome gift for me?" Wei Wuxian chuckled, waving it off. "Fine, fine, you didn't touch a drop, I believe you! Let's drop it. Come on, let me see how many cups it takes to knock out a pristine, tee-totaling Lan disciple!"

He filled a shallow bowl to the brim. Without missing a beat, Lan Wangji took it, tilted his head back, and downed the contents in one fluid gulp.

Wei Wuxian leaned in with bated breath, eyes glued to the man's face, waiting for the slightest blush of crimson to creep across those fair cheekbones. Yet after half a minute of staring, Lan Wangji’s expression remained an impenetrable block of stone, his pale amber eyes staring back with chilling clarity—completely, utterly sober!

Just as a wave of disappointment hit, and Wei Wuxian opened his mouth to egg him on for round two, Lan Wangji’s brow pinched slightly. He reached up, pressing a thumb against his temple. A second later, his elbow rested on the wood, his palm propping up his forehead, and his eyes drifted shut.

...Asleep?

He actually passed out cold!

Normally, when a person knocks back that much raw alcohol, they get sloshed first, act a fool, andthenpass out. How on earth did Lan Wangji bypass the entire intoxication phase and skip straight to sleep mode?!

The drunken spectacle was the whole damn point!

Wei Wuxian waved a hand before that rigidly upright, sleeping face, then clapped sharply right next to his ear.

Not a flinch.

A one-cup lightweight.

Slapping his forehead in defeat, Wei Wuxian sighed, hoisted Lan Wangji's limp right arm over his shoulder, and half-dragged, half-steered the immaculate Second Young Master out into the cool night air.

Having grown embarrassingly familiar with the layout of Lan Wangji's robes, he fished out the coin pouch, checked them into an inn for two private suites, and dumped the man onto a bed. He kicked off Lan Wangji's snow-white boots, tucked the quilt up to his chin, and slipped out the window into the dark.

Hiking out to a desolate patch of weeds beyond the town outskirts, Wei Wuxian drew the crude bamboo flute from his sash. Bringing the polished mouthpiece to his lips, he loosed a low, haunting melody across the wasteland, then lowered the wood and waited.

Over these past few weeks, he and Lan Wangji had been joined at the hip, leaving him zero room to sneak off and summon Wen Ning. Beyond keeping his identity under wraps, there was another reason.

Wen Ning had Lan blood on his hands. No matter how gentle Lan Wangji was toward him now, Wei Wuxian simply couldn't bring himself to whistle that terrifying war hound to heel in the man's presence. Or rather, it wasbecauseLan Wangji had treated him with such gentle patience that Wei Wuxian lacked the shamelessness to summon the ghost before his eyes. Thick-skinned as he was, even he had boundaries.

A faint, metallic rattle drifted through the cold air.

Clink. Clank.

Wen Ning stood with his chin dipped, his silhouette melting into the shadow cast by the ancient ramparts ahead.

Draped in tattered black, he blended seamlessly into the gloom, save for those stark, pupil-less expanses of white that burned through the shadows with chilling vacancy.

Hands clasped behind his back, Wei Wuxian walked a slow circle around him.

Wen Ning shifted, his feet shuffling as if trying to turn with his master's steps.

"Stay put," Wei Wuxian commanded softly.

The corpse instantly froze, looking like a chastised puppy, that gentle face sagging into a deeper, melancholic gloom.

"Hands."

Wen Ning raised his right arm obediently. Seizing the wrist, Wei Wuxian lifted it to the moonlight, carefully inspecting the thick black iron bands and heavy links clamped around the flesh.

This was no ordinary scrap metal. When Wen Ning flew into a frenzy, his bare hands could wring refined steel into damp clay; there was no way he would tolerate dragging chains around unless they had been specifically forged with high-grade warding seals to suppress his monstrous strength.

Reduced to ash and scattered to the winds?

If certain great clans were greedy enough to piece together a shattered Yin Tiger Tally, of course they would salivate over the prospect of leashing the legendary Ghost General. Who would ever bear to burn him to ash?

A cold sneer tugged at Wei Wuxian's mouth. Stepping up to Wen Ning’s flank, he raised his hands and began combing his fingers slowly through the corpse's tangled black hair.

Whoever had hoarded and chained Wen Ning needed a compliant weapon, not an independent mind. To force an unyielding fierce corpse to take orders, you had to hollow out his sanity, which meant embedding a spiritual spike directly into his skull. Sure enough, after pressing three distinct acupoints along the crown, Wei Wuxian’s fingertips brushed against a tiny, solid lump nestled near the right temple. Shifting his other hand to the matching point on the left side, his thumb caught the identical edge of a metallic pin.

Pinching the tips with both hands, Wei Wuxian pulled with slow, steady pressure, easing two long black spikes straight out of Wen Ning’s skull.

The needles measured a few inches long, slender as the red silk cord used to hang jade pendants, buried deep into the bone. The instant they cleared the bone, Wen Ning's features spasmed, fine webs of black capillaries throbbing across his dead-white sclera as his jaws clamped shut against a wave of phantom agony.

Dead as he was, the nervous memory of pain still lingered in the flesh.

Intricate, microscopic sealing scripts were etched along the length of both needles—clearly the handiwork of a master craftsman. Nursing Wen Ning back to full cognitive awareness was going to take time. Stashing the black spikes into his robes, Wei Wuxian glanced down at the chains wrapping the corpse's wrists and ankles. Letting him wander the realm clanking like an iron foundry wasn't an option; he needed an elite spiritual blade to sever the enchanted links.

Naturally, his thoughts went straight to Bichen. Borrowing a Lan heirloom to liberate Wen Ning felt a little blasphemous, but it was the only top-tier sword sitting within arm's reach, and he couldn't leave the boy dragging fifty pounds of iron behind him forever.

Here's the plan,Wei Wuxian mused.I'll slip back to the inn. If Lan Zhan is awake, I won't touch it. If he's still dead to the world, I'll borrow Bichen for a quick chop.

Minds made up, he wheeled around to leave.

And froze.

Standing motionless three paces behind him, cloaked in the midnight breeze, was Lan Wangji.
